claims.text: Spotify reports a total time saving of 60–90% on migrations done with its background coding agent (Honk) compared with writing the code by hand.
Spotify's Fleet Management system runs source-to-source transformations as jobs in a containerized environment, which automatically open pull requests against the target repositories.

Spotify's Fleet Management worked well for bumping dependencies in build files (e.g., Maven POMs), updating configuration files such as deployment manifests, and simple refactors such as removing or replacing a deprecated method call.

Spotify's Honk agent migrations include language modernization (replacing Java value types with records), breaking-change upgrades (data pipelines to the newest Scio), UI component migrations (the new Backstage frontend system), and schema-conforming YAML/JSON config changes.
Spotify states that the ROI of an automated change continues to increase as it is scaled out to more codebases over time.

Spotify slotted LLM agents into its existing fleet automation system, which already handled repo targeting, opening PRs and managing reviews, giving it the lowest marginal investment among the adopters compared.
Migrations at Spotify that previously required about 20K lines of hand-coded AST transforms can now be defined in natural language.

Spotify exposes its background coding agent via MCP so tasks can be started from Slack and GitHub Enterprise; an interactive workflow agent gathers context, builds a prompt, and hands it to the coding agent, which produces a pull request.

Spotify splits roles across agents: workflow agents handle ambiguity and context-gathering, the coding agent executes with minimal context (prompt and code), and review agents verify output before merge.
Spotify's Honk uses a small, fixed tool set: a verify tool, a limited git tool, and allow-listed shell commands.

Spotify's verification loop combines deterministic verifiers (syntax, build, tests) with an LLM-as-a-judge to prevent scope creep; the judge caught roughly a quarter of problematic changes, and the agent course-corrected in half of those cases.

Spotify's agents run in containers with limited permissions, minimal binary access and virtually no access to surrounding systems; Spotify deliberately limited agent flexibility to make behavior more predictable.
At QCon London 2026, Spotify said the LLM judge had been removed because it was too rigid and blocked correct changes; as models improved, verification built into the prompt was sufficient.

Per a secondary analysis, about 50% of Spotify's PRs were automated before the AI agent arrived, and the agent extended automation beyond what deterministic transformations could do; API token cost is estimated at $0.75 to $2.50 per PR.
At QCon London 2026, Spotify engineers said Honk merged 1,000 pull requests every 10 days and that human review had become the bottleneck.
Ramp built its agent so it can verify its own work: it runs tests, queries Sentry and Datadog, toggles feature flags and takes screenshots.

Ramp reported 30% of merged PRs in its frontend and backend repos came from agents within months, and a single security sweep found and fixed about 100 vulnerabilities, including high-severity IDORs that pen testing had missed.

Ramp's Inspect went from about 30% of merged PRs (January 2026) to about half (February, per Modal) to 74% (October, per co-founder Karim Atiyeh), with 99% of engineering, design and product staff using it in the past month and 3.4x PRs per builder versus a year earlier.

Ramp runs a sandboxed VM per session integrated with Sentry, Datadog, LaunchDarkly, Braintrust, GitHub, Slack and Buildkite, rebuilds repository images every 30 minutes, and gives each session its own database.
Ramp opens each pull request with the requester's own GitHub token so nobody can approve their own change, and tracks the share of sessions that end in a merged PR as its key metric.
Shopify's River agent went from 6% to 61% of merged mobile pull requests, using a remote mobile dev environment where the agent attaches screenshots and recordings.

Uber built a central AI platform with specialized agents for code review, test generation, migrations and PR routing, with an MCP gateway that turns any internal endpoint into an MCP server via a config change.
Uber reports 92% of developers use agents monthly, its test generation agent ships 5,000+ unit tests per month, and AI compute costs are up 6x since 2024.
A Linear customer story reports Ramp Inspect now writes three out of every four merged PRs and that the engineering bottleneck has shifted toward code review.
